Case Vignette: Michael (Age 27, Taxi Driver)

Michael settles into the chair, his large frame folding inward as if trying to occupy less space. He keeps his eyes on the floor, his hands resting on his knees, palms open. He speaks in a low, careful voice, as though testing whether it is safe to be heard. He has been driving for a ride-share company for three years, and he chose this work because it allows him to control his environment: he decides who enters his car, when to end a ride, and when to go home.

He grew up in a small town in West Africa, the eldest of four children. His father was a respected man in the community, a deacon at their church. At home, however, Michael says his father was a different person. The beatings began when Michael was about six years old, usually for small things: a forgotten chore, a wrong answer to a question, a look his father deemed disrespectful. His father used a belt, a wooden spoon, or the flat of his hand. Michael learned to anticipate the violence by the way his father would loosen his tie after work, the sound of his key in the lock, the silence that fell over the house. He learned to read the room the way a driver reads the road-for hazards, for escape routes.

The physical pain was not what stayed with him. It was the unpredictability. He could never know which version of his father would come through the door. He describes spending whole afternoons in a state of vigilance, listening for footsteps, monitoring his father's tone of voice, rehearsing answers to questions that had not yet been asked. His mother would sometimes step in, but she was often afraid too. Michael learned early that no one was coming to help.

Now, at twenty-seven, Michael lives alone in a one-bedroom apartment. He has never had a long-term romantic relationship. He says he does not trust people enough to let them get close. In his work, he keeps conversations brief. He has a standard script: greeting, confirmation of destination, a few polite remarks about traffic or weather. If a passenger asks personal questions, he changes the subject or goes quiet. He has developed a system for managing his anxiety: he always parks with his car facing the exit, he never accepts rides to unfamiliar neighborhoods after dark, and he keeps his phone on the passenger seat so he can see who is approaching before they reach the door.

The nightmares started in childhood and have never stopped. He dreams of being chased through a dark house, of a hand reaching for him from behind a door. He wakes frequently, his heart pounding, his sheets drenched in sweat. He sleeps in a corner of his bed, pressed against the wall, because it feels safer. He avoids alcohol because it makes the dreams worse. He has not visited his family in five years. When his mother calls, he lets it go to voicemail. He tells himself he will call back tomorrow, but tomorrow never comes.

His score on the PCL-5 is 56, which reflects the severity of his symptoms: the hypervigilance that never leaves him, even in his own home; the avoidance of memories and people; the negative beliefs about himself that have calcified into something he barely questions anymore. He believes he is fundamentally broken. He believes that if people really knew him, they would leave. He describes himself as "damaged goods," and he says this without irony, as though stating a simple fact about the weather.

In session, he is cooperative but cautious. He watches my face for signs of judgment. He apologizes when he cries. He says he does not know why he is still affected by something that happened so long ago. He says other people had it worse. He says he should be over it by now. He does not say this with anger, but with a kind of tired resignation, as though he has been carrying a weight for so long that he has forgotten what it feels like to put it down.
